GENITOURINARY / SEXUAL HEALTH__Urethral:
Genital discharge splits first by sex and site.
  • In men, a urethral discharge is urethritis: profuse and purulent suggests gonorrhoea, while scant and mucoid suggests non-gonococcal urethritis (usually chlamydia) (see gonorrhoea, chlamydia, urethritis (NGU)).
  • In women, most discharge is physiological or non-sexually-transmitted: thick, white, “cottage-cheese” with itch is candida; thin, grey, fishy-smelling is bacterial vaginosis; frothy, yellow-green with itch is trichomonas (see candidiasis, bacterial vaginosis).
  • A mucopurulent discharge from the cervix with post-coital bleeding is cervicitis (chlamydia / gonorrhoea). The key escalation is ascending infection: deep pain, fever and cervical excitation mean pelvic inflammatory disease (see pelvic inflammatory disease).
  • Whatever the cause, take a full sexual-health screen and arrange partner notification.
🚨Do not miss the ascending and the systemic. Pelvic inflammatory disease — deep pelvic pain, deep dyspareunia, fever and cervical motion tenderness — threatens fertility (tubal damage, ectopic risk) and is treated empirically without waiting for swabs (see pelvic inflammatory disease). Gonorrhoea is increasingly antibiotic-resistant (always culture) and can disseminate (arthritis, pustular rash) (see gonorrhoea). A pregnant woman with discharge and pain needs an ectopic pregnancy excluded, and a neonate with purulent conjunctivitis (ophthalmia neonatorum) needs urgent treatment for gonococcal / chlamydial infection. Always take a full STI screen (HIV, syphilis), consider a retained tampon / foreign body, and remember safeguarding in the young or vulnerable.

1Confirm & classify
🚩Pelvic inflammatory disease
  • Deep pelvic pain, deep dyspareunia, fever and cervical motion tenderness; mucopurulent cervix
  • Ascending chlamydia / gonorrhoea → tubal damage, infertility, ectopic risk (see pelvic inflammatory disease)
  • Treat empirically — do not wait for swab results
🟠Gonorrhoea
  • Profuse, purulent urethral or cervical discharge + dysuria; may be asymptomatic in women
  • Increasingly antibiotic-resistant — always culture (not just NAAT) (see gonorrhoea)
  • Can disseminate: arthritis, tenosynovitis, pustular rash; causes ophthalmia neonatorum
🟠Chlamydia / NGU
  • Scant, mucoid urethral discharge; the commonest STI — often asymptomatic
  • Non-gonococcal urethritis (chlamydia, Mycoplasma genitalium) (see chlamydia, urethritis (NGU))
  • Complications: PID, epididymo-orchitis, reactive arthritis, tubal infertility
🍶Candidiasis
  • Thick, white, “cottage-cheese” discharge + vulval itch and soreness; no offensive odour
  • Not sexually transmitted; commoner in diabetes, pregnancy, after antibiotics (see candidiasis)
  • Vulval erythema / fissuring; diagnosis is largely clinical
🐟Bacterial vaginosis
  • Thin, grey-white, homogeneous discharge with a fishy odour; little itch or inflammation
  • Overgrowth of anaerobes (loss of lactobacilli); not an STI (see bacterial vaginosis)
  • Raised vaginal pH >4.5, clue cells; associated with preterm birth in pregnancy
🦠Trichomonas & other
  • Frothy, yellow-green, offensive discharge + itch; “strawberry cervix” (trichomonas — an STI)
  • Cervicitis: mucopurulent cervical discharge + post-coital bleeding (chlamydia / gonorrhoea)
  • Consider a retained tampon / foreign body, and physiological discharge (see dysuria)
Sex, site, and the character of the discharge. In men, purulent = gonorrhoea and mucoid = chlamydia/NGU. In women, white + itch = candida, grey + fishy = BV, green + frothy = trichomonas. Layer on deep pain + fever + cervical excitation and you have PID — treat empirically.

Colour and smell narrow it fast. Purulent urethral discharge is gonorrhoea; cottage-cheese is candida; fishy grey is BV; green and frothy is trichomonas. But swabs and a full STI screen are mandatory — co-infection is common and much is asymptomatic.
3Assess & act
At the bedside — character of the discharge, examine, and screen fully
History & red flags
Colour / consistency / odour, itch, dysuria, deep pelvic pain / dyspareunia, fever, inter-menstrual / post-coital bleeding, a full sexual history (partners, sites, condom use), pregnancy, and safeguarding concerns
Examine
Inspect the discharge and genital skin; in women a speculum (cervix, os discharge, contact bleeding) and bimanual for cervical excitation and adnexal tenderness; in men the urethral meatus; check for a foreign body and examine joints / skin if disseminated infection is suspected
Investigate
NAAT for chlamydia & gonorrhoea (first-pass urine in men, vulvovaginal swab in women) plus gonococcal culture (resistance); vaginal pH, microscopy / wet-mount (clue cells, hyphae, motile trichomonads); a full STI screen (HIV, syphilis); pregnancy test; urine dip for UTI overlap
Act
Treat by cause: ceftriaxone for gonorrhoea, doxycycline for chlamydia/NGU, metronidazole for BV / trichomonas, topical / oral antifungal for candida; empirical antibiotics for PID. Always arrange partner notification, offer screening for other STIs, and give safety-net / abstinence advice

The rules that carry it: split by sex and site, read the colour and smell, but always take a NAAT + full STI screen because co-infection and asymptomatic carriage are common. Treat PID empirically to protect fertility, culture gonorrhoea, and never forget partner notification.

GENITOURINARY / SEXUAL HEALTH__Genital U:
The genital ulcer question is painful versus painless (and single versus multiple).
  • Painful, multiple, shallow ulcers preceded by vesicles are genital herpes — the commonest cause (see HSV (genital)).
  • A painless, solitary, indurated ulcer with a clean base (a chancre) is primary syphilis until proven otherwise — highly infectious, and the gateway to systemic disease (see syphilis).
  • Tropical / less-common causes split the same way: painful, ragged, undermined ulcers with suppurative inguinal buboes are chancroid; a small painless ulcer then large buboes is LGV.
  • Remember the non-infective causes — Behçet’s (recurrent oral + genital ulcers + uveitis), aphthous ulcers, fixed drug eruption and trauma — and the one you must not miss: a chronic, indurated, non-healing ulcer is penile or vulval carcinoma until biopsied.
  • Whatever the cause, test for HIV — any genital ulcer breaches the barrier and raises transmission (see HIV).
🚨Three things change the plan. A painless, indurated chancre is primary syphilis — highly infectious, and if untreated it progresses to secondary and tertiary disease; in pregnancy it risks congenital syphilis, so treat and screen (see syphilis). A chronic, indurated, non-healing ulcer with a rolled or everted edge is a penile / vulval carcinoma until a biopsy says otherwise. And every genital ulcer is an HIV opportunity: ulcers increase HIV transmission and a painful ulcer with fever, rash and lymphadenopathy may be seroconversion — always test, and consider PEP / PrEP (see HIV). Take a full STI screen and consider safeguarding.

1Confirm & classify
🚩Primary syphilis
  • Painless, solitary, indurated ulcer (chancre) with a clean base; non-tender rubbery nodes
  • Highly infectious; progresses to secondary / tertiary disease if untreated (see syphilis)
  • Dark-ground microscopy + treponemal serology; treat and screen (congenital risk in pregnancy)
🚩Penile / vulval carcinoma
  • Chronic, indurated, non-healing ulcer with a rolled / everted edge; older patient, HPV-related
  • Biopsy any persistent or atypical ulcer — do not treat blindly as infection
  • May have hard inguinal lymphadenopathy
🟠HIV / seroconversion
  • Test everyone — genital ulcers increase HIV transmission and acquisition
  • Seroconversion: painful ulcer + fever, rash, lymphadenopathy after exposure (see HIV)
  • Offer PEP after high-risk exposure and PrEP for prevention
🟠Genital herpes
  • Painful, multiple, shallow ulcers preceded by vesicles; tender inguinal nodes; recurrent
  • First episode can be severe (dysuria, retention, systemic upset) (see HSV (genital))
  • Diagnose with an HSV PCR swab of the lesion
🟠Chancroid & tropical
  • Chancroid: painful, ragged, undermined ulcer + suppurative inguinal buboes (H. ducreyi)
  • LGV: small painless ulcer then large buboes (groove sign); granuloma inguinale: beefy-red ulcer
  • Consider with travel / relevant exposure; confirm and treat as per GUM
🔎Non-infective
  • Behçet’s: recurrent oral + genital ulcers + uveitis + pathergy
  • Aphthous ulcers, fixed drug eruption (recurs at the same site), trauma / dermatoses
  • Crohn’s can cause genital / perianal ulceration
Painful vs painless carries it. Painful + vesicles + multiple = herpes; painless + solitary + indurated = syphilis. A chronic, indurated, non-healing ulcer is cancer until biopsied — and every genital ulcer earns an HIV test.

Tender and crops, or single and hard? A tender crop of ulcers on an erythematous base is herpes; a single, hard, painless ulcer is a syphilitic chancre. When an ulcer will not heal or looks atypical, biopsy it — and test for HIV and the rest regardless.
3Assess & act
At the bedside — painful or painless, the edge, the nodes, the skin
History & red flags
Painful or painless?, single vs multiple, preceding vesicles, duration and healing, systemic upset (fever, rash), a full sexual history (partners, sites, travel), drugs, recurrent oral ulcers, and safeguarding concerns
Examine
Characterise the ulcer — base, edge, induration, tenderness; inspect the whole ano-genital area and mouth / eyes (Behçet’s); palpate inguinal nodes (tender vs rubbery, fluctuant buboes); look for a rash on palms and soles (secondary syphilis)
Investigate
HSV PCR swab of the lesion; syphilis dark-ground microscopy + treponemal serology; an HIV test (4th-generation; window ~45 days, repeat at 6–12 weeks) and a full STI screen (chlamydia / gonorrhoea NAAT window ~2 weeks); biopsy any chronic / atypical / non-healing ulcer; consider chancroid / LGV testing with relevant exposure
Act
Treat by cause: aciclovir for herpes, benzathine penicillin for syphilis, GUM-directed therapy for chancroid / LGV; refer suspected carcinoma for biopsy and oncology. GENITOURINARY / SEXUAL HEALTH__Genital L:
Most genital lumps are benign — the job is to spot the few that are not.
  • The commonest pathological lump is anogenital warts: soft, fleshy, painless, cauliflower-like or filiform papules from HPV (see HPV / genital warts).
  • Two look-alikes matter. Pearly, dome-shaped, umbilicated papules are molluscum contagiosum. Broad, flat, moist, warty plaques (condylomata lata) are secondary syphilis — a completely different, highly infectious diagnosis, so do syphilis serology (see syphilis).
  • Recognise the normal variants that frighten patients — pearly penile papules (rows around the corona), Fordyce spots and vestibular papillomatosis — and the cystic lumps (epidermoid cysts, a Bartholin’s cyst / abscess).
  • The one you must not miss: a solitary, hard, ulcerated or non-healing lump (or a pigmented, changing one) is a penile / vulval carcinoma or melanoma until biopsied.
🚨Biopsy the sinister, and do not mistake syphilis for warts. A solitary, hard, ulcerated, bleeding or non-healing lump — or a pigmented, irregular, changing one — may be a penile / vulval carcinoma or melanoma and must be biopsied, not frozen or ignored. Condylomata lata (flat, moist plaques) are secondary syphilis, not ordinary warts — highly infectious and systemic, so send serology (see syphilis). A tense, painful posterior-labial swelling is a Bartholin’s abscess → incision & drainage / marsupialisation. Take a full STI screen, offer HPV vaccination and cervical screening (anal screening only in high-risk groups), consider HIV / immunosuppression if warts or molluscum are florid (see HIV), and consider safeguarding if a child has anogenital warts.

1Confirm & classify
🚩Carcinoma / melanoma
  • Solitary, hard, ulcerated, bleeding or non-healing lump; or a pigmented, changing lesion
  • Biopsy any persistent or atypical lump — do not freeze or treat blindly
  • Older, HPV-related (penile / vulval SCC); hard inguinal nodes suggest spread
🟠Condylomata lata (syphilis)
  • Broad, flat, moist, warty plaques in warm folds — not ordinary warts
  • A feature of secondary syphilis: rash on palms / soles, mucous patches (see syphilis)
  • Highly infectious → confirm with syphilis serology and treat / trace
🟠Anogenital warts (HPV)
  • Soft, fleshy, painless, cauliflower-like or filiform papules; may be multiple
  • Low-risk HPV (6, 11); the commonest pathological genital lump (see HPV / genital warts)
  • Full STI screen; offer HPV vaccination and cervical screening (anal screening only in high-risk groups)
🟣Molluscum contagiosum
  • Pearly, dome-shaped, umbilicated papules with a central dimple; painless
  • Poxvirus; florid / atypical in adults → consider HIV / immunosuppression (see HIV)
  • Usually self-limiting; diagnosis is clinical
🟠Bartholin’s cyst / abscess
  • Unilateral swelling at the posterior labia (4 / 8 o’clock); soft cyst or tense, painful abscess
  • Abscess → incision & drainage / marsupialisation (± antibiotics)
  • Recurrent or in older women → consider biopsy to exclude carcinoma
🩺Cysts & normal variants
  • Pearly penile papules (rows around the corona), Fordyce spots, vestibular papillomatosis — normal
  • Epidermoid / sebaceous cysts: smooth, mobile, may have a punctum
  • Scabetic nodules: itchy penile / scrotal papules with burrows (see scabies)
Warty, pearly, cystic, or hard? Soft fleshy cauliflower = HPV warts; pearly umbilicated = molluscum; flat moist plaques = condylomata lata (syphilis — do serology); rows around the corona = a normal variant. A solitary hard / ulcerated / pigmented lump earns a biopsy.

GENITOURINARY / SEXUAL HEALTH__Testicula:
A discrete testicular lump — usually found by the patient on self-examination — is answered by one question: is it arising from the testis, or separate from it?
  • A solid lump arising from the body of the testis that does not transilluminate, in a man aged 15–35, is testicular cancer until an ultrasound proves otherwise (see testicular cancer).
  • A lump that is clearly separate from the testis is almost always benign — an epididymal cyst (above and behind, transilluminates) or a varicocele (“bag of worms”) (see scrotal lumps).
  • A tender lump with fever or dysuria is epididymo-orchitis (see epididymo-orchitis); a sudden, painful one is torsion — a surgical emergency (see acute scrotal pain). For the wider picture of a whole hemi-scrotum enlarging (fluid, hernia), see scrotal swelling.
  • The rule that saves lives here: examine the testis, and image any solid intratesticular lump.
🚨Never reassure a testicular lump without imaging. A painless, solid, intratesticular lump is testicular cancer until a scrotal ultrasound and tumour markers (AFP, β-hCG, LDH) say otherwise — it is the commonest solid cancer in young men and is highly curable when caught early (see testicular cancer). A reactive (secondary) hydrocele can hide a tumour, so image a firm or irregular testis even when there is surrounding fluid. A sudden, painful lump with a high-riding testis and absent cremasteric reflex is torsion → immediate exploration, not a scan (see testicular torsion, acute scrotal pain). Undescended testis and a family history raise cancer risk.

1Confirm & classify
🚩Testicular tumour
  • Painless, solid, arising from the testis, hard / irregular, does not transilluminate; ages 15–35
  • Urgent scrotal ultrasound + tumour markers (AFP, β-hCG, LDH) (see testicular cancer)
  • A reactive hydrocele can hide it — image a firm testis; risk ↑ with undescended testis
🚩Testicular torsion
  • Sudden, painful swelling, high-riding testis, absent cremasteric reflex, nausea
  • Immediate exploration (within ~6 h) — do not wait for imaging (see acute scrotal pain)
  • The lump here is the swollen, tender testis itself
🟠Epididymo-orchitis
  • Tender lump / swelling of the epididymis, fever, dysuria / discharge, relieved by elevation
  • Young → STI (chlamydia, gonorrhoea); older → coliform / UTI (see epididymo-orchitis)
  • A tender lump is inflammatory until torsion is excluded
💧Epididymal cyst / spermatocele
  • Separate from the testis, above and behind it, transilluminates, painless
  • A benign fluid-filled lump; confirm with ultrasound (see scrotal lumps)
  • Treat only if symptomatic or the diagnosis is uncertain
🟠Varicocele
  • “Bag of worms” above the testis, usually left, decompresses lying flat; dull ache / subfertility
  • New, right-sided or non-decompressing → image the kidneys (renal mass) — see scrotal swelling
  • Separate from the testis; the testis itself is normal
🩺Benign & mimics
  • The normal epididymis / appendix testis mistaken for a lump; reassure after examination
  • A hydrocele (fluid surrounding the testis) — a whole-scrotum swelling (see scrotal swelling)
  • Teach testicular self-examination for early detection
From the testis, or separate? A solid lump arising from the testis that does not transilluminate is cancer until ultrasound proves otherwise. A lump that is clearly separate (above / behind, transilluminating, or a bag of worms) is benign. A tender or sudden painful lump means infection or torsion.

How and when the lump was found, pain (sudden = torsion), change in size, fever / dysuria, weight loss, back pain, a previous undescended testis, subfertility, and family history of testicular cancer
Examine
Is it arising from or separate from the testis?; transillumination; consistency (solid vs fluctuant); tenderness; can you get above it; the cremasteric reflex and lie; examine the abdomen and lymph nodes and the chest if metastatic spread is suspected
Investigate
Scrotal ultrasound (with Doppler) is the key test for any solid or uncertain lump; tumour markers (AFP, β-hCG, LDH) for a suspected tumour; urine dip + first-pass urine NAAT / MSU for suspected epididymo-orchitis; staging CT if a tumour is confirmed

Refer a solid intratesticular lump urgently to urology (radical inguinal orchidectomy + oncology; sperm banking first). Treat epididymo-orchitis with antibiotics; explore suspected torsion immediately; reassure and offer surgery for symptomatic epididymal cysts / varicoceles; teach self-examination

GENITOURINARY / SEXUAL HEALTH__Erectile:
Erectile dysfunction is often the first sign of cardiovascular disease. The small penile arteries narrow before the coronaries, so ED can precede angina or a heart attack by years — every man with ED needs his cardiovascular and metabolic risk assessed (see cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes). The first split is organic versus psychogenic. Organic ED is gradual and global, with loss of early-morning and nocturnal erections — think vascular (commonest), neurogenic, endocrine or drug-induced. Psychogenic ED is sudden and situational, with preserved nocturnal / early-morning erections and a clear stressor or relationship context (see depression). A focused history, a few bloods (HbA1c, lipids, morning testosterone) and a medication review resolve most cases — and PDE5 inhibitors work well once the cause is addressed.
🚨Treat ED as a cardiovascular and endocrine warning, not just a bedroom problem. New ED is an independent marker of cardiovascular risk — assess blood pressure, lipids, HbA1c and smoking, and ask about angina and claudication (see acute coronary syndrome, peripheral arterial disease). ED is a common presenting feature of diabetes — check the glucose (see type 2 diabetes). Low libido + fatigue suggests hypogonadism (check a morning testosterone); galactorrhoea or a visual-field defect suggests hyperprolactinaemia / a pituitary tumour (see hyperprolactinaemia). Do not forget drugs (antihypertensives, antidepressants, finasteride) and note that PDE5 inhibitors are contraindicated with nitrates.

  • Sudden onset, situational, with preserved nocturnal / early-morning erections
  • Performance anxiety, relationship difficulty, depression (see depression)

GENITOURINARY / SEXUAL HEALTH__Haematosp:
Haematospermia — blood in the semen — is alarming to the patient but usually benign. The whole approach is stratify by age and red flags. In a man under 40 with a single or few episodes and no red flags, it is almost always self-limiting and idiopathic (or post-inflammatory) — examine, dip the urine and reassure. The concern is the man over 40, or persistent / recurrent haematospermia, or one with red flags (visible haematuria, an abnormal prostate, weight loss, LUTS) — here you must exclude prostate and genitourinary cancer (see prostate cancer, abnormal prostate on DRE, haematuria). The commonest identifiable cause is infection / inflammation of the prostate or seminal tract (prostatitis, seminal vesiculitis, STI) (see urinary tract infection). Do not forget bleeding tendency / anticoagulants, uncontrolled hypertension, and iatrogenic causes (after a prostate biopsy or vasectomy).
🚨Age and persistence decide the work-up. In a man over 40, or with persistent / recurrent haematospermia, examine the prostate (DRE) and check a PSA to exclude prostate cancer (see prostate cancer, abnormal prostate on DRE). Haematospermia with visible haematuria needs the haematuria pathway — exclude bladder and upper-tract malignancy (see haematuria, bladder cancer). Consider a bleeding disorder or an anticoagulant (see anticoagulation), and uncontrolled hypertension (see hypertension). In those with relevant travel / exposure, think genitourinary tuberculosis or schistosomiasis (see tuberculosis). Persistent, unexplained haematospermia warrants MRI of the prostate / seminal vesicles and urological referral.

GENITOURINARY / SEXUAL HEALTH__Dyspareun:
Dyspareunia — pain with intercourse — is localised first: superficial or deep? Superficial (entry) dyspareunia is pain at the introitus on penetration — think vulvovaginal infection (candida, herpes), atrophic vaginitis of the menopause, vulval dermatoses (lichen sclerosus / planus), and vaginismus (see candidiasis, menopause). Deep dyspareunia is pain on deep penetration from a pelvic cause — endometriosis / adenomyosis, pelvic inflammatory disease, fibroids or ovarian pathology (see benign uterine & pelvic conditions, pelvic inflammatory disease). Take a careful history (is it new, situational, cyclical?), examine (inspect the vulva, speculum, bimanual for tenderness and masses), and swab. The red flags to exclude are gynaecological malignancy (a pelvic mass, post-coital or postmenopausal bleeding) and PID (see gynaecological cancers). Much superficial dyspareunia is highly treatable once the cause is named.
🚨Deep dyspareunia with sinister company needs urgent work-up. Deep pain with a pelvic mass, post-coital or intermenstrual / postmenopausal bleeding, or weight loss may be a gynaecological cancer (see gynaecological cancers) — examine and image (and take a smear / biopsy of a suspicious cervix). Deep pain with vaginal discharge, fever and cervical motion tenderness is pelvic inflammatory disease — treat empirically to protect fertility (see pelvic inflammatory disease, vaginal discharge). Sudden severe pelvic pain with an adnexal mass could be ovarian torsion or a ruptured cyst. And always consider the context of the pain — a history of sexual trauma / assault, and safeguarding, may underlie the presentation.

GENITOURINARY / SEXUAL HEALTH__Anogenita:
Anogenital itch or rash is sorted into infective, inflammatory or neoplastic. Most is inflammatory — irritant / contact dermatitis (soaps, wipes, moisture) is the commonest, with eczema, inverse psoriasis and lichen simplex from the itch-scratch cycle (see contact dermatitis, eczema, psoriasis). Infective causes include candida (satellite lesions), tinea cruris, threadworm (nocturnal perianal itch in children), scabies, pubic lice and warts (see candidiasis, scabies, genital lumps & warts). Two things must not be missed: lichen sclerosus (white, atrophic, “figure-of-eight” skin with a small cancer risk) (see benign vulvovaginal conditions), and neoplasia — a persistent, non-healing, thickened, pigmented or steroid-unresponsive plaque may be VIN, squamous cell carcinoma, extramammary Paget’s or melanoma and needs a biopsy (see gynaecological cancers). And generalised itch can reflect systemic disease.
🚨Biopsy the plaque that will not settle. A persistent, thickened, ulcerated, pigmented or non-healing anogenital lesion — especially one that fails to respond to topical steroids — may be vulval / anal intraepithelial neoplasia, squamous cell carcinoma, extramammary Paget’s disease or melanoma and must be biopsied (see gynaecological cancers). Lichen sclerosus is itchy, white and atrophic with a figure-of-eight distribution and fissuring; it needs a potent topical steroid and monitoring because of a small risk of vulval carcinoma (see benign vulvovaginal conditions). Generalised pruritus with weight loss, jaundice or lymphadenopathy points to a systemic cause (diabetes, iron deficiency, cholestasis, renal failure, lymphoma) — check the bloods. And consider safeguarding and abuse where the pattern fits.

🩺Systemic pruritus
  • Generalised itch: diabetes (recurrent candida), iron deficiency, cholestasis
  • Chronic kidney disease, thyroid disease, lymphoma (with weight loss / night sweats)
  • Check FBC, ferritin, glucose / HbA1c, LFTs, U&E, TFTs
Infective, inflammatory, or neoplastic? Most is inflammatory (contact dermatitis is commonest); infective causes are swabbed and treated. But a persistent, non-healing, steroid-unresponsive lesion is biopsied — and don’t miss lichen sclerosus.

The pattern names it. Satellite lesions = candida; annular + central clearing = tinea; figure-of-eight white skin = lichen sclerosus; symmetrical after a product = contact dermatitis. Anything that persists or fails topical steroids earns a biopsy.
3Assess & act
At the bedside — inspect the pattern, swab, and biopsy the persistent
History & red flags
Site and duration, localised vs generalised itch, nocturnal (threadworm, scabies), new products / soaps / wipes, over-washing, discharge, bowel symptoms, systemic features (weight loss, jaundice), diabetes, and any non-healing area
Examine
Inspect the whole anogenital skin — demarcation, scale, satellite lesions, white atrophic change, fissures, ulceration, pigmentation or thickening; examine other sites (scalp, nails, finger webs) and general skin; note perianal tags / haemorrhoids
Investigate
Skin swab / scrapings (candida, dermatophyte) and microscopy; a tape test for threadworm; patch testing for suspected contact allergy; biopsy any persistent, atypical or steroid-unresponsive lesion; systemic bloods (FBC, ferritin, glucose / HbA1c, LFTs, U&E, TFTs) for generalised pruritus
Act
Remove irritants and use an emollient / soap substitute; treat infection (antifungal, permethrin for scabies, anti-helminthic for threadworm); topical steroids for dermatoses (potent for lichen sclerosus, with monitoring); break the itch-scratch cycle; refer / biopsy for suspected neoplasia and investigate systemic pruritus
Then — confirm the cause
Neoplasia → biopsyLichen sclerosus → clinical (± biopsy)Candida / tinea → swab / scrapings (microscopy)Threadworm → tape test / clinicalContact dermatitis → history (± patch testing)Systemic pruritus → FBC, ferritin, glucose, LFTs, U&E
The rules that carry it: classify infective / inflammatory / neoplastic, remove irritants and restore the skin barrier, treat the organism or dermatosis, and biopsy anything persistent or steroid-unresponsive. Recognise lichen sclerosus, and screen for a systemic cause if the itch is generalised.
